ch52.title: Nineteen Appearances
ch52.b002: Resurrection Sunday was a terrible day in the lives of the apostles. Ten of them spent the larger part of it in the upper chamber behind barred doors, afraid that the agents of the Sanhedrin would arrest them if they were found abroad. Their isolation had much to do with their troubles. John Mark brought them the rumors from about the temple, but it did not occur to him to gather news from the groups of believers to whom Jesus had already appeared. That had always been the work of David’s messengers, and they were all gone on their last assignment. For the first time the apostles realized how much they had depended on those runners for word of the kingdom’s affairs.
ch52.b003: All day long John upheld the idea that Jesus had risen; he recounted no fewer than five times when the Master had said he would rise again. Peter vacillated between faith and doubt. He could not forget the grave cloths lying in the tomb as if the body had simply evaporated from within. He would grow sorrowful, thinking that perhaps Jesus stayed away because of him, who had denied him in Annas’s courtyard, and then cheer himself with the women’s message, “Go tell my apostles—and Peter.” Nathaniel’s philosophic counsel was often the only sustaining influence in the room. Simon Zelotes lay on a couch in a corner with his face to the wall and scarcely spoke. Philip, usually so quiet, asked questions all afternoon, especially whether a risen body would bear the marks of the crucifixion. Matthew worried over their finances, now that Judas was gone and David had turned the funds over to him. One of the Alpheus twins spoke for both: “⟦Q 191:0.11⟧We do not understand about the resurrection, but our mother says she talked with the Master, and we believe her.⟦/Q⟧” Thomas, meanwhile, brooded alone at Bethpage. He wanted to go back, but having left as he did, he was too proud to return so soon.
ch52.b005: A little after eight that evening Peter ventured out into the courtyard of the Mark home, thinking to remove himself from among his brethren lest his presence prevent the Master from coming to them. He had lived under a heavy burden of guilt since his denial; he had shuddered at the fate of Judas and wondered whether he was still an apostle at all. As he strolled among the flowers and shrubs, he thought of the loving look the Master had given him as he passed by on Annas’s porch, and of the words, “Go tell my apostles—and Peter.” His faith began to surmount his doubts. He stood still, clenching his fists, and spoke aloud: “⟦Q 191:1.2⟧I believe he has risen from the dead; I will go and tell my brethren.⟦/Q⟧”
ch52.b006: As he said this, there suddenly appeared before him the form of a man, who spoke in familiar tones: “⟦Q 191:1.2⟧Peter, the enemy desired to have you, but I would not give you up. I knew it was not from the heart that you disowned me; therefore I forgave you even before you asked; but now must you cease to think about yourself and the troubles of the hour while you prepare to carry the good news of the gospel to those who sit in darkness. No longer should you be concerned with what you may obtain from the kingdom but rather be exercised about what you can give to those who live in dire spiritual poverty.⟦/Q⟧” For almost five minutes they walked through the garden and talked of things past, present, and future. Then the Master vanished, saying, “⟦Q 191:1.3⟧Farewell, Peter, until I see you with your brethren.⟦/Q⟧” It was his eighth morontia manifestation.
ch52.b007: Peter rushed up to the upper chamber, breathless: “⟦Q 191:1.4⟧I have seen the Master; he was in the garden. I talked with him, and he has forgiven me.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles were about ready to surrender their doubts when Andrew rose and warned them not to be too much influenced by his brother, intimating that Peter had seen things before that were not real. Deeply hurt, Peter lapsed into crestfallen silence, and the twins went over to tell him that they believed him.
ch52.b008: Nine O’Clock in the Upper Room
ch52.b009: Shortly after nine, when Cleopas and Jacob had gone, while the twins comforted Peter and Nathaniel remonstrated with Andrew, and with every door bolted for fear of arrest, the Master suddenly appeared in the midst of the ten: “⟦Q 191:2.1⟧Peace be upon you. Why are you so frightened when I appear, as though you had seen a spirit? Did I not tell you about these things when I was present with you in the flesh?… How long will you doubt my words and refuse to believe my promises? And now that you actually see me, will you believe? Even now one of you is absent. When you are gathered together once more, and after all of you know of a certainty that the Son of Man has risen from the grave, go hence into Galilee. Have faith in God; have faith in one another; and so shall you enter into the new service of the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Then he vanished in an instant, and they all fell on their faces, praising God. This was the ninth appearance.
ch52.b010: The next day, Monday, Jesus spent wholly with the more than one million morontia directors and transition mortals who had come to Urantia from the mansion worlds of Satania. About midnight his morontia form was adjusted for the second stage of morontia progression, and he went on stage by stage: to Jerusem citizenship on May 7, and into the embrace of the Most Highs of Edentia on May 14. As he advanced, it became more and more difficult to make him visible to mortal eyes.
ch52.b012: A little after eight o’clock on Tuesday evening, April 11, at Philadelphia, Abner and Lazarus were opening a special meeting in the synagogue to discuss the crucifixion and the report of the resurrection. As they stood together in the pulpit, the whole audience of some one hundred and fifty believers saw the Master appear between them, though neither of the two observed him. He stepped forward and said: “⟦Q 191:4.3⟧You are to love all men as I have loved you; you are to serve all men as I have served you.… Remember, as you love one another, all men will know that you are my disciples.⟦/Q⟧” Early the next morning these believers went forth proclaiming that Jesus had risen. It was the tenth appearance.
ch52.b013: Thomas spent a lonesome week in the hills around Olivet. On Saturday night, April 15, Peter and John found him and brought him back. The next day he heard all the stories, but he steadfastly refused to believe, maintaining that Peter had enthused them into imagining it. At supper a little after six, with Peter on one side of him and Nathaniel on the other, he said: “⟦Q 191:5.2⟧I will not believe unless I see the Master with my own eyes and put my finger in the mark of the nails.⟦/Q⟧” The doors were shut and barred. Suddenly the morontia Master appeared inside the curvature of the table, standing directly in front of Thomas: “⟦Q 191:2.1,191:5.3⟧Peace be upon you.… As the Father sent me into the world, so send I you.… I send you forth, not to love the souls of men, but rather to love men.… The Jews have extolled goodness; the Greeks have exalted beauty; the Hindus preach devotion; the faraway ascetics teach reverence; the Romans demand loyalty; but I require of my disciples life, even a life of loving service for your brothers in the flesh.⟦/Q⟧”
ch52.b014: Then he looked down into the face of Thomas. He reminded him that, though he saw no nail marks, since the Master was raised in the form Thomas too would one day have, already in his heart he had begun to believe. “⟦Q 191:5.4⟧Your doubts, Thomas, always most stubbornly assert themselves just as they are about to crumble. Thomas, I bid you be not faithless but believing—and I know you will believe, even with a whole heart.⟦/Q⟧” Thomas fell on his knees and exclaimed, “⟦Q 191:5.5⟧I believe! My Lord and my Master!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said: “⟦Q 191:5.5⟧You have believed, Thomas, because you have really seen and heard me. Blessed are those in the ages to come who will believe even though they have not seen with the eye of flesh nor heard with the mortal ear.⟦/Q⟧” Then, moving toward the head of the table, he told them all to go to Galilee, and vanished. This was the eleventh appearance. Very early the next morning, before the break of day, the eleven started out for Galilee.
ch52.b015: On Tuesday evening, April 18, in Alexandria, Rodan and some eighty believers had gathered to hear Nathan of Busiris, the fifth runner in David’s Jerusalem-to-Alexandria relay, tell the story of the crucifixion. Nathan ended with these words: “⟦Q 191:6.1⟧But David, who sends us this word, reports that the Master, in foretelling his death, declared that he would rise again.⟦/Q⟧” Even as he spoke, the Master appeared in full view of all: “⟦Q 191:2.1,191:6.2,191:6.3⟧Peace be upon you.… This gospel of the kingdom belongs to both Jew and gentile, to rich and poor, to free and bond, to male and female, even to the little children.… it shall not be committed to the custody of mere priests.⟦/Q⟧” This was the twelfth appearance. Two days later, when David’s herald of the resurrection arrived, they answered him: “⟦Q 191:6.4⟧Yes, we know, for we have seen him.⟦/Q⟧”
ch52.b016: Morning on the Sea of Galilee
ch52.b017: The apostles reached Bethsaida late on Wednesday night, John Mark with them, for he had followed them out of the city and boldly joined them beyond Bethany. They waited at the Zebedee home through Thursday, and then Peter proposed that they go fishing, and they all went. All night they toiled and caught nothing. About six o’clock on Friday morning, April 21, as their boat neared the usual landing, they saw someone on the beach standing by a fire. At first they thought it was John Mark, but the man was too tall. He called to them, “Lads, have you caught anything?” They answered, “No.” He said, “⟦Q 192:1.3⟧Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find fish.⟦/Q⟧” They did so, and the net was filled until they could hardly draw it up. John Zebedee, quick of perception, leaned over and whispered to Peter, “It is the Master,” and Peter cast himself into the water to reach his side the sooner.
ch52.b018: John Mark, running down the beach, counted eleven men instead of ten, guessed who the stranger was, and was the first to kneel at his feet: “My Lord and my Master.” Jesus answered him, not with “Peace be upon you” as in Jerusalem, but in commonplace tones: “⟦Q 192:1.4⟧Well, John, I am glad to see you again and in carefree Galilee, where we can have a good visit. Stay with us, John, and have breakfast.⟦/Q⟧” Peter had been shocked for a moment at the sight of the coals glowing on the beach, so like the midnight charcoal fire in the courtyard of Annas where he had disowned his Master, but he shook himself and knelt: “My Lord and my Master!” They hauled in the catch and counted 153 large fish. There was no miracle in it; the Master simply knew the fish were there. John Mark dressed seven of them, Jesus put them on the fire, broke the bread, and at last served the lad himself. And as they ate, he recounted their many experiences in Galilee and by this very lake. This was the thirteenth appearance.
ch52.b020: After breakfast Jesus walked up and down the beach with them two and two. To John he said, “John, do you love me?” When John answered, “⟦Q 192:2.1⟧Yes, Master, with all my heart,⟦/Q⟧” the Master said: “⟦Q 192:2.1⟧Then, John, give up your intolerance and learn to love men as I have loved you. Devote your life to proving that love is the greatest thing in the world.⟦/Q⟧” Three times he asked Peter whether he loved him. The third time Peter, slightly grieved at the Master’s seeming distrust, said with considerable feeling, “⟦Q 192:2.4⟧Lord, you know all things, and therefore do you know that I really and truly love you.⟦/Q⟧” Then said Jesus: “⟦Q 192:2.4⟧Feed my sheep. Do not forsake the flock. Be an example and an inspiration to all your fellow shepherds.… And follow after me even to the end.⟦/Q⟧” Peter took this literally and, pointing to John, asked, “⟦Q 192:2.5⟧If I follow on after you, what shall this man do?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said: “⟦Q 192:2.5⟧Peter, be not concerned about what your brethren shall do. If I will that John should tarry after you are gone, even until I come back, what is that to you? Only make sure that you follow me.⟦/Q⟧”
ch52.b021: To Andrew, the former chief of the apostles, he said, “⟦Q 192:2.7⟧Andrew, if you trust me, trust your brethren more—even Peter,⟦/Q⟧” and asked him to be a wise counselor to James his brother in the flesh when heavy burdens should fall on him in the days of persecution. James Zebedee he urged to cultivate patience; Thomas to cease doubting and grow in faith; Nathaniel to “⟦Q 192:2.10⟧admix friendship with your counsel and add love to your philosophy.⟦/Q⟧” Philip and Matthew were to busy themselves no more with money and goods but go forth preaching. To the Alpheus twins he said: “⟦Q 192:2.13⟧Never forget that, when you are a faith son of God, all upright work of the realm is sacred. Nothing which a son of God does can be common. Do your work, therefore, from this time on, as for God.⟦/Q⟧” It was almost ten o’clock when he took leave of them: “⟦Q 192:2.14⟧Farewell, until I meet you all on the mount of your ordination tomorrow at noontime.⟦/Q⟧” Simon Zelotes, who had grown so despondent that he had gone home on reaching Bethsaida, was brought back that same day by Peter and Andrew.
ch52.b022: The Mount of Ordination and the Five Hundred
ch52.b023: At noon on Saturday, April 22, the eleven knelt in a circle about the Master on the very hill near Capernaum where he had first set them apart. He repeated the charges and re-enacted the ordination, but when he prayed, it was in tones of majesty and with words of power such as they had never before heard. This was the fourteenth appearance. Then no one saw him for a full week. On Saturday afternoon, April 29, more than five hundred believers gathered by the seaside at Bethsaida to hear Peter’s first public sermon since the resurrection. Peter ended: “⟦Q 192:4.3⟧We affirm that Jesus of Nazareth is not dead; we declare that he has risen from the tomb; we proclaim that we have seen him and talked with him.⟦/Q⟧” Just then, by his side, in full view of all, the Master appeared and said, “⟦Q 192:4.3⟧Peace be upon you, and my peace I leave with you.⟦/Q⟧” It was the fifteenth appearance.
ch52.b024: The apostles returned to Jerusalem, arriving late on May 3. It was a sad homecoming for John Mark, for a few hours before, his father, Elijah Mark, had suddenly died. The apostles made the upper chamber their headquarters, and there on Thursday night all except Thomas, Simon Zelotes, and the twins pledged themselves to go forth preaching the risen Lord. Nathaniel opposed the change, but he could not withstand Peter’s eloquence. So, ere the Master had ascended, his well-meaning representatives began the subtle process of changing the religion of Jesus into a new and modified form of religion about Jesus.
ch52.b026: About nine o’clock on Friday night, May 5, in the courtyard of Nicodemus, the Jerusalem believers met together for the first time since the resurrection: the eleven, the women’s corps, and about fifty other disciples. Suddenly the Master stood in full view and taught them: “⟦Q 193:0.4,193:0.5⟧Your message is not changed by my resurrection experience. Sonship with God, by faith, is still the saving truth of the gospel of the kingdom.… Only tarry here in Jerusalem while I go to the Father, and until I send you the Spirit of Truth.⟦/Q⟧” It was near daybreak before they dispersed. This was the sixteenth appearance.
ch52.b027: On the Sabbath afternoon of May 13 he appeared to Nalda and about seventy-five Samaritan believers near Jacob’s well at Sychar: “⟦Q 193:1.2⟧It is your faith that saves your souls. Salvation is the gift of God to all who believe they are his sons.⟦/Q⟧” On the evening of May 16 at Tyre he told the believers: “⟦Q 193:2.2⟧The fact that the dead rise is not the gospel of the kingdom.… the fruits of the divine spirit which are yielded in the lives of spirit-born and God-knowing mortals are: loving service, unselfish devotion, courageous loyalty, sincere fairness, enlightened honesty, undying hope, confiding trust, merciful ministry, unfailing goodness, forgiving tolerance, and enduring peace.⟦/Q⟧” These believers had known him in the flesh, and while his friends could not readily recognize his morontia form, they were never slow to identify his personality when he spoke.
ch52.b029: Early on Thursday morning, May 18, as the eleven were about to sit down to breakfast in the upper chamber, Jesus made his last appearance as a morontia personality. He reminded them to tarry in Jerusalem until he sent the Spirit of Truth. Simon Zelotes interrupted: “⟦Q 193:3.2⟧Then, Master, will you restore the kingdom, and will we see the glory of God manifested on earth?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 193:3.2⟧Simon, you still cling to your old ideas about the Jewish Messiah and the material kingdom. But you will receive spiritual power after the spirit has descended upon you, and you will presently go into all the world preaching this gospel of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” He spoke of Judas, who was no more with them “⟦Q 193:3.2⟧because his love grew cold, and because he refused to trust you, his loyal brethren,⟦/Q⟧” and he ended: “⟦Q 193:3.2⟧Trust, therefore, and confide in one another. And this is all the more needful since I am this day going to leave you alone in the world. The hour has come; I am about to go to the Father.⟦/Q⟧”
ch52.b030: Then he beckoned them to come with him and led them out toward the Mount of Olives. Not a word was spoken by any of them from the time they left the upper chamber until Jesus paused with them on the mountainside.
ch53.title: Ascension and Pentecost
ch53.b002: On that Thursday morning, May 18, the eleven followed their Master in silence out of the upper chamber and up toward the Mount of Olives. In the first part of his farewell message Jesus alluded to the loss of Judas, and he held up the tragic fate of their traitorous fellow worker as a solemn warning against the dangers of social and fraternal isolation.
ch53.b003: Judas went wrong primarily because he was very markedly an isolated personality, shut in and away from ordinary social contacts. He persistently refused to confide in, or freely fraternize with, his fellow apostles. Yet that alone would not have destroyed him had he not also failed to increase in love and grow in spiritual grace, and had he not harbored grudges and fostered the craving to “get even” with somebody for all his disappointments. That he need not have gone wrong is well proved by Thomas and Nathaniel, who were cursed with the same sort of suspicion and overdeveloped individualism; even Andrew and Matthew had leanings in that direction. But all these men grew to love Jesus and their fellows more, and not less, as time passed, and slowly they learned to trust and confide in their brethren. Judas, whenever his emotional conflicts built up, went instead to his unspiritual relatives or to chance acquaintances who were indifferent or hostile to the kingdom, and received from them only unwise consolation.
ch53.b004: As a child, life had been made too easy for him; he bitterly resented thwarting, always expected to win, and was a very poor loser. He never acquired a philosophic technique for meeting disappointment, and instead of accepting it as a commonplace feature of human existence, he unfailingly blamed someone else. He did not like to face facts frankly. In all the years of their association he never once went to the Master with a purely personal problem. And he never learned that the real rewards of noble living are spiritual prizes, not always distributed during this one short life in the flesh. “⟦Q 193:4.13⟧In life, he ignored those who loved him, and in death, he was friendless.⟦/Q⟧”
ch53.b006: It was almost half past seven when Jesus arrived on the western slope of Mount Olivet with his eleven silent and somewhat bewildered apostles. From this place, about two thirds of the way up the mountain, they could look out over Jerusalem and down upon Gethsemane. As he stood before them, without being directed they knelt about him in a circle, and the Master said:

ch53.b007.en: “I bade you tarry in Jerusalem until you were endowed with power from on high. I am now about to take leave of you; I am about to ascend to my Father, and soon, very soon, will we send into this world of my sojourn the Spirit of Truth; and when he has come, you shall begin the new proclamation of the gospel of the kingdom, first in Jerusalem and then to the uttermost parts of the world. Love men with the love wherewith I have loved you and serve your fellow mortals even as I have served you. By the spirit fruits of your lives impel souls to believe the truth that man is a son of God, and that all men are brethren. Remember all I have taught you and the life I have lived among you. My love overshadows you, my spirit will dwell with you, and my peace shall abide upon you. Farewell.”

ch53.b008: When the morontia Master had thus spoken, he vanished from their sight. This so-called ascension was in no way different from his other disappearances from mortal vision during the forty days of his morontia career; the one who had stood before them simply was no longer seen. It was about seven forty-five that morning. The Master went to Edentia by way of Jerusem, where the Most Highs, under the observation of the Paradise Son, released Jesus of Nazareth from the morontia state and returned him, through the spirit channels of ascension, to the status of Paradise sonship and supreme sovereignty on Salvington.
ch53.b010: At Peter’s direction John Mark and others went out to call the leading disciples together at the home of Mary Mark. By half past ten, one hundred and twenty of the foremost disciples living in Jerusalem had gathered. Among them were Mary the mother of Jesus, who had come back from Galilee with John Zebedee, and James the brother of Jesus. It was the first conference of the Master’s disciples since the end of his planetary career. Peter spoke for the eleven and gave a thrilling report of their last meeting with the Master, touchingly portraying his farewell and his disappearance. Then he explained that a successor to Judas was to be chosen from two men who had been suggested, Matthias and Justus. The eleven went downstairs and cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias. He was inducted as the new apostle and appointed treasurer, though he had little part in the later activities of the apostles. Just about noon they returned to the upper chamber with the news, and Peter called all the believers to prayer, that they might be prepared to receive the gift of the spirit which the Master had promised to send.
ch53.b011: One O’Clock in the Upper Room
ch53.b012: About one o’clock, as the one hundred and twenty were engaged in prayer, they all became aware of a strange presence in the room. At the same time they all became conscious of a new and profound sense of spiritual joy, security, and confidence. This new consciousness of spiritual strength was immediately followed by a strong urge to go out and publicly proclaim the gospel of the kingdom and the good news that Jesus had risen from the dead. Peter stood up and declared that this must be the coming of the Spirit of Truth which the Master had promised, and he proposed that they go to the temple and begin to proclaim the good news committed to them. And they did just what he suggested.
ch53.b013: There was no form or ceremony in it. When the spirit came upon them, they were simply sitting there, having just been engaged in silent prayer. Nor did the gift come only to the apostles. The one hundred and twenty men and women in the upper chamber all received the new teacher, and when the spirit descended at Jerusalem, the same thing happened in Philadelphia, in Alexandria, and wherever true believers dwelt, indeed to all the honest of heart throughout the whole world. The mother and brother of Jesus were there among the others and received no more of the good gift than did their fellows. Prayer did not bring the spirit, but it had much to do with determining the capacity of each believer to receive it; it “⟦Q 194:3.20⟧does so often dig out larger and deeper channels wherein the divine bestowals may flow.⟦/Q⟧”
ch53.b014: The Temple Sermon and the Pool of Siloam
ch53.b015: It happened to be the Jewish festival of Pentecost, and thousands of visitors from all parts of the world were in Jerusalem, many of them having stayed on since the Passover. The apostles, who had been in hiding for forty days, now emerged to appear boldly in the temple. About two o’clock Peter stood up in that very place where his Master had last taught in the temple and delivered an impassioned appeal. Six apostles took part—Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, and Matthew. They talked for more than an hour and a half, in Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic, and even a few words in other tongues with which they had some speaking acquaintance. The Jewish leaders were astounded at their boldness, but they feared to molest them because so many believed their story. By half past four more than two thousand new believers followed the apostles down to the pool of Siloam, where Peter, Andrew, James, and John baptized them in the Master’s name. It was dark when they had finished baptizing that multitude.
ch53.b017: The spirit never creates a consciousness of himself, only a consciousness of Michael, the Son. He came to foster and personalize truth, to destroy the believer’s feeling of orphanhood now that Jesus had gone, to help men recall and understand the Master’s words, and to lead all believers into all truth. The Creator Son, in the flesh, revealed God to men; the Spirit of Truth, in the heart, reveals the Creator Son to men. Since that day man has lived under a threefold spirit endowment: the spirit of the Father, the Thought Adjuster; the spirit of the Son, the Spirit of Truth; and the spirit of the Spirit, the Holy Spirit.
ch53.b018: On the day of Pentecost the religion of Jesus broke all national restrictions and racial fetters. Woman stood before God on an equality with man, and the belief in special priesthoods and sacred families came to an end. The spirit was bestowed in the country as well as in the city; no lonely place or years of solitary meditation were needed to receive it. “⟦Q 194:3.13⟧Up to Pentecost, religion had revealed only man seeking for God; since Pentecost, man is still searching for God, but there shines out over the world the spectacle of God also seeking for man and sending his spirit to dwell within him when he has found him.⟦/Q⟧” It had looked dark on the day of the crucifixion, but it was gloriously bright on the resurrection morning, and still brighter and more joyous on the day of Pentecost.
ch53.b019: Before Pentecost the apostles had given up homes, families, friends, worldly goods, and positions for Jesus. At Pentecost they gave themselves to God, and the Father and the Son responded by giving themselves to man, sending their spirits to live within men. This experience of losing self and finding the spirit was not one of emotion; it was an act of intelligent self-surrender and unreserved consecration. Pentecost endowed mortal man with the power to forgive personal injuries, to keep sweet in the midst of the gravest injustice, to remain unmoved in the face of appalling danger. The teachers of the new religion were to go out to conquer the world with unfailing forgiveness, matchless good will, and abounding love—to overcome evil with good and vanquish hate by love. Urantia has passed through great and destructive wars, and all who took part in them met with defeat. Only one came out of those struggles with an enhanced reputation: Jesus of Nazareth and his gospel of overcoming evil with good.
ch53.b021: Yet in that moment of spiritual ecstasy and personal triumph, the greatest news these men could think of was the fact of the risen Master. They had been taught that the gospel was the fatherhood of God and the sonship of man, but now they went forth preaching salvation through Jesus, and they unintentionally stumbled into the error of substituting some of the facts associated with the gospel for the gospel message itself. Peter unwittingly led off in this mistake, and others followed him on down to Paul, who created a new religion out of the new version of the good news. These mistakes of the intellect did not hinder their growth in spirit. In less than a month after the Spirit of Truth came, the apostles made more individual spiritual progress than during their almost four years of loving association with the Master. And the new message about Jesus carried with it many of the fundamental truths of the gospel of the kingdom, truths which, sooner or later, will emerge to transform the civilization of all mankind.
ch53.b022: A new fellowship was arising in the world. Day by day the believers continued with one accord in the temple and broke bread at home. They called each other brother and sister, ministered to the poor, and, confidently expecting Jesus to return within their generation, shared their goods in common. When the Sadducees began to put the leaders in jail, the rabbi Gamaliel advised them: “⟦Q 194:4.10⟧Refrain from these men and let them alone, for if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them, lest haply you be found even to be fighting against God.⟦/Q⟧” A time of peace followed, and the new gospel spread rapidly. Then two pupils of Rodan came from Alexandria and won many converts among the Hellenists, Stephen and Barnabas among them. Stephen and his Greek associate began to preach more as Jesus taught, and in one of Stephen’s public sermons the Jewish rulers dispensed with all formalities of trial and stoned him to death on the spot. He became the first martyr to the new faith.
ch53.b023: Within one month of Stephen’s death the church at Jerusalem was organized under the leadership of Peter, and James the brother of Jesus was installed as its titular head. Then broke out new and relentless persecutions, and the teachers of the new religion about Jesus, which afterward at Antioch was called Christianity, went forth to the ends of the empire. They followed the path of Alexander’s march of former days, by way of Gaza and Tyre to Antioch, then over Asia Minor to Macedonia, and on to Rome and the uttermost parts of the empire.
ch54.title: The Faith of Jesus
ch54.b002: The results of Peter’s preaching on the day of Pentecost decided the future course of most of the apostles. Peter was the real founder of the Christian church; Paul carried the Christian message to the gentiles, and the Greek believers carried it to the whole Roman Empire. The tradition-bound Hebrews, as a people, refused both Jesus’ gospel and the apostles’ proclamation of the risen Christ. But the Western world of that day was intellectual, war weary, and thoroughly skeptical of all existing religions and philosophies. Heirs of great achievements in philosophy, art, literature, and politics, its peoples had no soul-satisfying religion, and their spiritual longings remained unsatisfied. Upon such a stage the teachings of Jesus, embraced in the Christian message, were suddenly thrust, and a new order of living was presented to hungry hearts.
ch54.b003: The Hellenization of Christianity started in earnest on the day the Apostle Paul stood before the council of the Areopagus in Athens and told the Athenians about “the Unknown God.” The Greek revered beauty, the Jew holiness, but both peoples loved truth. At first the Romans fought Christianity while the Greeks embraced it, and it was the Greeks who later forced the Romans to accept the new religion as a part of Greek culture. The early Romans were honest, zealous, and dedicated, but without a religion worthy of the name; their unparalleled honesty, devotion, and stalwart self-control was ideal soil for the growth of Christianity. The Roman provided a unity of political rule; the Greek, a unity of culture and learning; Christianity, a unity of religious thought and practice.
ch54.b005: Wisely or unwisely, the early leaders of Christianity deliberately compromised the ideals of Jesus in an effort to save and further many of his ideas. They made compromises with Mithraism, and later generations adopted so much of the ritualistic pageantry of paganism that even the emperor Constantine was won to the new religion. Yet the Christians gained the ascendancy in that a new and far higher note in human morals was struck, a greatly enlarged concept of God was given to the world, the hope of immortality became part of a recognized religion, and “⟦Q 195:0.17⟧Jesus of Nazareth was given to man’s hungry soul.⟦/Q⟧” It was a Greek from Egypt, Athanasius, who stood up so fearlessly at Nicaea that the assembly dared not obscure the concept of the nature of Jesus. By the end of the second century practically all the great minds of the Greco-Roman world had become Christian.
ch54.b006: The teaching of Christ’s love for children soon ended the widespread practice of exposing unwanted infants, particularly girl babies, to death. What gave greatest power to Christianity was the way its believers lived lives of service and even the way they died for their faith in the times of persecution. Still, even a good religion could not save a decaying empire. In the so-called dark ages the church shared in the decline; religion became monasticized, asceticized, and legalized. But Christianity persisted through the long night of Western civilization and was still functioning as a moral influence when the renaissance dawned. Its history, beginning in the unintended transformation of the religion of Jesus into a religion about Jesus and passing through Hellenization, paganization, institutionalization, hibernation, rejuvenation, and fragmentation, is indicative of inherent vitality and vast recuperative resources.
ch54.b007: A River from the Galilean Highlands
ch54.b008: Now religion faces the challenge of scientific minds, materialism, and a secularism that ignores God. But modern science has left true religion—the teachings of Jesus as translated in the lives of his believers—untouched; all it has done is to destroy the childlike illusions of the misinterpretations of life. “⟦Q 195:6.11⟧A machine cannot know, much less know truth, hunger for righteousness, and cherish goodness.⟦/Q⟧” Indeed, “⟦Q 195:7.13⟧a self-conscious and avowed mechanist is the best possible answer to mechanism.⟦/Q⟧” And secularism, for all the liberties won in its revolt against ecclesiastical domination, cannot bring peace: “⟦Q 195:8.11⟧You simply cannot establish the brotherhood of men while ignoring or denying the fatherhood of God.⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b009: The stream of modern Christianity drains many an ancient pagan swamp and barbarian morass, as well as the high Galilean tablelands which are supposed to be its exclusive source. “⟦Q 195:10.1⟧Christianity has indeed done a great service for this world, but what is now most needed is Jesus.⟦/Q⟧” The world needs to see Jesus living again on earth in the experience of spirit-born mortals. It is not the first mile of compulsion, duty, or convention that will transform man and his world, but the second mile of free service and liberty-loving devotion, and there are so few genuine second-milers. The hope of modern Christianity is that it should humbly bow itself before the cross it so valiantly extols, “⟦Q 195:10.21⟧there to learn anew from Jesus of Nazareth the greatest truths mortal man can ever hear—the living gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man.⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b011: Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God. He experienced the ordinary ups and downs of mortal existence, but he never religiously doubted the certainty of God’s watchcare and guidance. His faith was neither traditional nor merely intellectual; it was wholly personal and purely spiritual. He did not cling to it as a struggling soul at war with the universe, nor use it merely as a consolation in difficulty. Rather, he felt the tremendous thrill of living, by faith, in the very presence of the heavenly Father, and even in the face of apparent defeat and an ignominious death he calmly stood in the divine presence, free from fear.
ch54.b012: Jesus trusted God much as the child trusts a parent, and he had a profound confidence in the universe, just such a trust as the child has in its home. He combined the stalwart and intelligent courage of a full-grown man with the sincere and trusting optimism of a believing child. It is not strange that he once said, “⟦Q 196:0.12⟧Except you become as a little child, you shall not enter the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” Yet his faith, though childlike, was in no sense childish. And despite his deep consciousness of close relationship with divinity, when addressed as Good Teacher, this Galilean instantly replied, “⟦Q 196:0.9⟧Why do you call me good?⟦/Q⟧” In such splendid self-forgetfulness we begin to understand how the Universal Father could so fully reveal himself through him.
ch54.b013: His indomitable faith never became fanatical, for it never ran away with his balanced judgments about family love, social duty, and economic necessity. Jesus never prayed as a religious duty. To him prayer was a declaration of soul loyalty, an expression of thanksgiving, a prevention of conflict, a vindication of moral decision, and “⟦Q 196:0.10⟧the mighty mobilization of the combined soul powers to withstand all human tendencies toward selfishness, evil, and sin.⟦/Q⟧” The secret of his unparalleled religious life was this consciousness of the presence of God, and he attained it “⟦Q 196:0.10⟧by intelligent prayer and sincere worship—unbroken communion with God—and not by leadings, voices, visions, or extraordinary religious practices.⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b015: No matter how great the fact of the sovereignty of Michael, the human Jesus must not be taken away from men. He has ascended on high as a man as well as God; he belongs to men, and men belong to him. Let not discussions of the humanity or divinity of the Christ obscure the saving truth that Jesus of Nazareth was a religious man who, by faith, achieved the knowing and the doing of the will of God; “⟦Q 196:1.1⟧he was the most truly religious man who has ever lived on Urantia.⟦/Q⟧” The time is ripe for the figurative resurrection of the human Jesus from his burial tomb amidst the theological traditions and dogmas of nineteen centuries, that he may be presented as the living Jesus to the church that bears his name and to all other religions.
ch54.b016: Just as men must progress from the consciousness of the human to the realization of the divine, so did Jesus ascend from the nature of man to the consciousness of the nature of God. The stages of that ascent were marked by the arrival of the Thought Adjuster, the messenger of Immanuel who appeared to him at Jerusalem when he was about twelve, the manifestations at his baptism, the experiences on the Mount of Transfiguration, the morontia resurrection, the spirit ascension, and the final embrace of the Paradise Father. This ascent was an exclusively mortal achievement, and when he had attained divinity, he was still the same human Jesus, the Son of Man as well as the Son of God.
ch54.b018: Jesus’ great contribution was not that he revealed so many new ideas about the Father, but that he so magnificently and humanly demonstrated a new and higher type of living faith in God. He does not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him. He challenged his followers not only to believe what he believed, but also to believe as he believed. “⟦Q 196:0.13⟧This is the full significance of his one supreme requirement, ‘Follow me.’⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b019: To follow him is not to imitate literally the outward life of Jesus in Galilee, but to share his faith: to trust God as he trusted God and to believe in men as he believed in men. He never argued about the fatherhood of God or the brotherhood of men; he was a living illustration of the one and a profound demonstration of the other. The common people heard him gladly because he was one of them, an unpretentious layman; the world’s greatest religious teacher was indeed a layman. “⟦Q 196:2.1⟧You may preach a religion about Jesus, but, perforce, you must live the religion of Jesus.⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b020: A Revelation That Shall Not Fail
ch54.b021: The Hebrews had a religion of moral sublimity; the Greeks evolved a religion of beauty; Paul and his conferees founded a religion of faith, hope, and charity. Jesus revealed and exemplified a religion of love: security in the Father’s love, with joy and satisfaction in sharing that love in the service of the human brotherhood. He led men to feel at home in the world and taught them that the world was not fundamentally evil. He saw most men as weak rather than wicked, more distraught than depraved, but no matter what their status, they were all God’s children and his brethren.
ch54.b022: He taught men to place a high value upon themselves in time and in eternity, and because of that high estimate he was willing to spend himself in the unremitting service of humankind. “⟦Q 196:2.10⟧What mortal can fail to be uplifted by the extraordinary faith Jesus has in him?⟦/Q⟧” Religion, as he lived it, does not remove human troubles, but it does “⟦Q 196:3.1⟧dissolve, absorb, illuminate, and transcend them.⟦/Q⟧” Science is man’s effort to solve the riddles of the material universe, and philosophy his attempt to unify human experience, but religion is “⟦Q 196:3.30⟧man’s supreme gesture, his magnificent reach for final reality, his determination to find God and to be like him.⟦/Q⟧”
ch54.b023: So the child of the carpenter’s home in Nazareth lived, and so he died, and so he rose and returned to his Father. His own ascent became “⟦Q 196:2.4⟧the new and living way whereby all mortals may so ascend from humanity to divinity.⟦/Q⟧”

ch54.b024.en: Be not discouraged; human evolution is still in progress, and the revelation of God to the world, in and through Jesus, shall not fail.

ch54.b025: When all is said and done, the Father idea is still the highest human concept of God.
